verdictReason: Need is real (Rule 204-2: copy of each advertisement kept 5 years), but the deciding facts could not be read: Patrina, Smarsh, Archive Intel, ArchiveSocial and PageFreezer pages were blocked this session and search budget was spent, so no incumbent price or web/social-only tier is verified. Verified: written communications must also be kept (email needed anyway), Meta social capture needs App Review plus Business Verification, only SEC-registered advisers ($100M+ AUM) are in scope, base year-1 profit about -$13, pessimistic about -$2.7k. Price/scope is not an edge. Leaning kill, not provable.

answers.question: (1) What free/cheap alternative covers the wedge?
answers.answer: Not re-verified this session: GitHub (ArchiveBox, Browsertrix) and all vendor pages (Patrina, Archive Intel, Smarsh, ArchiveSocial, PageFreezer, ustechautomations) were refused by the fetch tool (permission/provenance errors) and WebSearch budget was exhausted. What the rule text does show: it requires a copy of each advertisement kept in an easily accessible place for five years and names no vendor or format, so a manual PDF/screenshot routine is a legal status quo. The first attempt read ArchiveBox (MIT, self-hosted) and Browsertrix (AGPLv3, self-host or hosted) as free capture tools; that reading is not re-confirmed here, so treat them as likely but unconfirmed. Case-file items say Patrina is from $60/mo with no auto-renewing annual contract and Archive Intel advertises no retrieval fees; both unconfirmed. Whether any incumbent already sells web+social only at or below $29/mo is the open question.

answers.question: (2) What structural edge exists and who could copy it?
answers.answer: None verified. The scan-1 edge is price ($29 vs about $60) and narrow scope, which are not edges, and any incumbent could ship a web/social-only tier. The only compounding element is the accumulated 5-year archive per firm (switching cost) plus an exam-ready export, which is copyable and requires trust that a nameless founder lacks. A possible barrier is that social capture is gated by platform review (Meta needs App Review and Business Verification, see D31/D34/D35), but that gate applies equally to the entrant and was already cleared by incumbents, so it protects them, not the entrant. The buyer must also keep written communications (D24), so the product is a second-vendor add-on beside an email archive. Falsifier: an incumbent already sells web+social at or below $29, or RIAs refuse a second vendor.

answers.question: (3) Who demonstrably pays and how much?
answers.answer: The mandatory duty is verified: an SEC-registered adviser must keep a copy of each advertisement it disseminates (including a communication made to ten or more persons), and an advertisement is any communication to more than one person offering advisory services, so website and social posts are in scope. No primary evidence of payment or price was read this session; the only price data are unverified case-file items (Smarsh $15-35 per seat with annual minimum, Patrina from $60/mo, an advisor-website vendor that refers archiving to Global Relay, Presults or Smarsh). SEC registration generally starts at $100M AUM, so solo and small SEC-registered RIAs are a subset; smaller advisers fall under state rules that were not read.

answers.question: (4) Legal/platform constraints?
answers.answer: Rule 204-2(g)(3)(i) puts the duty to safeguard electronic records on the adviser, so a vendor claiming it is 'compliant' or 'exam-proof' without an audit takes on exposure; claims should be limited to describing capture, timestamp and export features. Social capture is the hard half. Meta Platform Terms: delete all Platform Data when the operator stops operating the product (a solo exit-risk clash with a 5-year promise, although a 'legitimate business purpose' reading may soften it). Meta App Review is required for apps used by anyone without a role on the app; Instagram Advanced Access needs App Review and Business Verification, covers professional accounts only, and a permission only reaches data created by the user who granted it; Facebook Page public content needs the same review and business verification. LinkedIn, X and YouTube terms could not be fetched. Scraping instead of APIs was not assessed and is likely a ToS breach.

answers.question: (5) Year-1 numbers?
answers.answer: Bottom-up with every volume an assumption: first revenue at day 65 (month 3), 2 new firms per month from month 3, 2% monthly churn from month 4, $29/mo flat, variable cost $7.25 per firm-month (scan-1 model figure, unsourced), $40/mo fixed tools (assumption), startup cash $1,750 counted as year-1 cost, owner time (12 h/week, about 620 h) not costed. Base: revenue about $2,957 (18 firms at month 12), cost about $2,969, profit about -$13. Pessimistic (price x0.8, 1 new firm per month, all costs x1.5): revenue about $1,183, cost about $3,899, profit about -$2,717. Not viable inside year 1 even before owner time; only the $100M+ AUM subset can be sold to.

killReasons.reason: Written communications must be kept as well, so the buyer needs an email archive anyway and a web/social-only product is at best a second-vendor add-on; this is an inference from the rule text, whether buyers accept a second vendor is unverified.

Social capture depends on platform gates: Instagram Advanced Access needs App Review and Business Verification, covers only professional accounts and only data the granting user created; Facebook Page content needs the same; Meta requires deleting Platform Data when the operator stops the product. A nameless solo entrant must pass these before first revenue at day 65 and incumbents already have, so the gate protects them. LinkedIn and X were not readable.
Pessimistic year-1 economics are clearly negative (about -$2.7k) and base case is about break-even before about 620 owner hours; volumes are assumptions, not sourced.
Buyer pool is the SEC-registered subset (threshold about $100M AUM); smaller advisers follow state rules that were not checked.
The adviser carries the duty to safeguard electronic records, so a vendor 'compliant' claim creates liability and the entrant can only describe capture features, which weakens trust-based selling.
